notes.title: Restrict reflection to the boundary; work through typed contracts
notes.core: Reflection is appropriate for dynamic discovery and specialized frameworks, but contain it at a trusted construction boundary. Check that the discovered implementation meets a known interface and invoke ordinary typed methods afterward.
rules: Prefer normal constructors, factories, and interfaces when the implementation is available at compile time.
When discovery is essential, validate an allowlisted Class and use asSubclass to establish the expected supertype before constructing.
Resolve an intentional public constructor with getConstructor rather than suppressing encapsulation through setAccessible.
Handle ClassNotFoundException, NoSuchMethodException, IllegalAccessException and InvocationTargetException as distinct operational diagnostics where useful.
Use ServiceLoader for discoverable provider contracts when the module/service model suits the application.
Keep runtime reflection failures outside request-processing hot paths; do not assume historical slowdown ratios apply to modern HotSpot.
nuance: Java 21 module strong encapsulation may deny access to non-open packages; a library cannot assume private fields can be opened reflectively.
Class.asSubclass checks the superclass/interface compatibility at runtime; generic type arguments remain erased.
Public constructors can still throw application exceptions; InvocationTargetException wraps the underlying cause.
ServiceLoader is not a universal replacement for runtime plugin names; provider registration and trust still matter.
Loading an arbitrary user-selected class is a trust and resource-control decision, not made safe by a cast alone.
notes.misconception: A class name plus unchecked reflective cast provides the same compile-time and access guarantees as a typed constructor.
notes.production_context: A merchant connector registry selects an explicitly configured provider, validates that it implements PaymentConnector, then executes payments through the typed interface without reflective request dispatch.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 retains strong JPMS encapsulation, Class.asSubclass and ServiceLoader; prohibited deep reflection should not be bypassed with broad --add-opens by default.

notes.title: Keep native boundaries minimal, reviewed and measured
notes.core: Use native interoperability only for a capability that cannot be met suitably through maintained Java APIs or for a measured and justified native dependency. A native call adds memory-safety, portability, lifecycle and debugging obligations.
rules: First inspect Java standard and maintained JVM libraries for platform or performance needs before introducing JNI.
Make native access an isolated adapter with explicit input/output ownership and lifetime; use a Java fallback when feasible.
Treat a native call as a trust boundary: validate sizes, encodings and lifecycle before crossing it.
Do not claim JNI automatically speeds hot paths; crossing boundaries and copying data can dominate small calls.
Plan target operating systems, architecture support, release packaging, failure handling and native-memory monitoring.
Run focused functional, fuzz and leak tests for native code rather than relying on Java type safety.
nuance: Java21 Foreign Function & Memory API was a preview API (JEP 442), not a universally stable production replacement; review version-specific deployment flags.
Panama/FFM in newer JDKs has different maturity from Java21; do not backport later guarantees to the 21 baseline.
Calling an external process via ProcessHandle/ProcessBuilder is distinct from in-process native memory access and has its own security/cancellation needs.
Java heap health does not alone prove native-memory absence of leaks; off-heap resources need explicit observation.
JNI remains reasonable for essential vendor drivers or accelerated library integration after tests and risk assessment.
notes.misconception: C++ behind JNI is inherently faster and just as memory safe as Java in the same process.
notes.production_context: A settlement reconciliation adapter isolates a required vendor native codec while Java validation, retry logic and business decisions remain in typed Java code.
notes.java21_delta: Java21 supports preview java.lang.foreign interop only with appropriate preview enablement; avoid documenting it as the final stable API of later JDKs.

notes.title: Optimize based on profiles without corrupting stable APIs
notes.core: Choose clear algorithms and durable API contracts first, then use measured production-representative evidence to locate actual bottlenecks. Make one controlled change at a time and compare outcomes against correctness and capacity targets.
rules: Identify the user-visible SLO and workload before deciding that a function needs tuning.
Instrument real hot paths using profiling/tracing and attribute CPU, allocation, lock time and I/O separately.
Look for algorithmic complexity problems before low-level instruction or allocation tweaks.
Preserve stable public and persisted formats; do not warp an API for a short-lived performance hypothesis.
Run comparative before/after benchmarks with warm-up, representative data and correctness checks, including p95/p99 when latency matters.
Allow rollback if regression, fairness or operational complexity outweighs the measured gain.
nuance: Microbenchmarks such as JMH isolate small operations but cannot alone predict end-to-end throughput or contention.
Java21 JIT, GC, CPU shape, virtual-thread scheduling and workload profile may make old runtime ratios irrelevant.
A fast average can coexist with slow tail latency and unacceptable memory spikes.
CPU saturation may be consequence or symptom; correlation between high CPU and latency does not prove direction.
Correctness invariants and observability must be preserved during optimization; avoid timing assertions with a fixed speedup.
notes.misconception: The most visually complicated Java method is the bottleneck, and its microbenchmark speedup proves production improvement.
notes.production_context: A checkout pipeline has a p99 regression: tracing implicates a queue stall rather than the arithmetic helper. The team validates queue depth and allocations before choosing a targeted change.
notes.java21_delta: Use current JFR/async-profiler and Java21-aware JMH methods; no Java9-era fixed optimization ratios can stand in for measurements.

notes.title: Use predictable names and APIs without ignoring local conventions
notes.core: Use idiomatic Java identifiers and meaningful grammatical names so clients can infer intent. Where framework conventions or stable public APIs require different forms, document the exception and preserve compatibility.
rules: Use lowercase dotted package names, UpperCamelCase type names and lowerCamelCase method/field names.
Use uppercase underscore-separated identifiers for true immutable constant fields rather than every static final mutable holder.
Name state-question methods is/has when natural; name actions with verbs and factories with consistent conventions.
Use descriptive type and parameter names at public boundaries; abbreviated local loop counters may be appropriate.
Distinguish toX conversions from asX views when they represent ownership versus sharing, and document mutability precisely.
Preserve JavaBeans get/set names where frameworks explicitly require them, rather than globally rewriting API methods.
nuance: Naming conventions guide maintainability; Java itself enforces only identifier syntax, not spelling quality.
Java21 record component accessors use componentName() (not generated getComponentName()), requiring awareness of reflection and bean libraries.
All-caps static final collection fields are not automatically deeply immutable; construction and content policies matter.
An @Override annotation helps discover mistaken method-name changes that silently introduce overloads.
Renaming public methods or serialized properties can change API compatibility even when new names read better.
notes.misconception: Anything declared static final is an immutable constant and an idiomatic name is safe to retrofit without compatibility tests.
notes.production_context: A Java21 record representing a merchant status uses clear accessors while a legacy bean DTO retains getStatus() for framework compatibility.
notes.java21_delta: Java21 records, sealed types, builders and JavaBeans-aware frameworks have distinct conventions; validate serialized property names before refactoring.

notes.title: Express ordinary state without exception-driven flow control
notes.core: Exceptions report exceptional failure; ordinary end-of-data and absence should use state tests or result types. Never disguise unrelated failures as normal termination by catching broad exceptions.
rules: Use ordinary loop conditions or enhanced-for instead of relying on an exception to stop iteration.
Use Iterator.hasNext before next in stable state; do not catch NoSuchElementException as the normal loop exit.
Offer Optional or a documented absence result when lack of a value is expected and regular.
Avoid state-test/act race in concurrent or externally mutable objects; use a single atomic attempt with a result type.
Catch only the exceptions that the boundary can intentionally recover from; preserve unrelated programming failures.
Keep exceptions informative for violation of explicit contracts rather than swallowing them for control flow.
nuance: An iterator can become invalid through concurrent modification despite a prior hasNext; ordinary testing is not a substitute for synchronization.
A queue whose contents can change asynchronously may need poll returning null/Optional as the atomic absence signal, not size()+remove().
Unchecked exception cost varies across JDK configurations; correctness and debuggability are the primary reasons to avoid using them as flow tokens.
Exceptions for genuinely invalid methods or unmet invariants are still appropriate, even if a caller can test first.
Not every absent return should use Optional (collections often return empty); keep semantics consistent with the earlier Item 55 guidance.
notes.misconception: Repeatedly throwing NoSuchElementException is a convenient equivalent to hasNext and masks no other issues.
notes.production_context: A consumer polls a concurrent reconciliation work queue, handling null as no task and propagating unexpected failures; a snapshot List is traversed normally.
notes.java21_delta: Java21 still offers Iterator.hasNext, Queue.poll and Optional; concurrency can make separate test/act operations unsafe, so distinguish linearizable poll from two-step checks.
